title: arXiv Trending AI — 6 November 2026
global_caveat: arXiv has no official trending chart; this ordering is inferred from sparse early attention and cross-checkable relevance signals. Citation evidence is limited for papers less than a day old, and independent replication remains outstanding.

sections.title: Scientist World: Grow a Research World for AI-Scientists
sections.abstract: The paper introduces an automated pipeline that turns research papers into executable environments for AI scientists, releasing 1,000 environments and reporting that frontier systems beat reproduced human methods in 74% of from-scratch attempts.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors present Scientist World as a benchmark, research-trace dataset, and training environment built from executable reproductions of published work; the paper reports 1,000 environments and 6,400 research-trace hours.
sections.unique_caveat: The headline model evaluation uses a fixed cohort of ten lower-compute environments rather than all 1,000 released environments, limiting how broadly the reported win rates generalize.
sections.evidence_for_ranking: Two same-day secondary writeups provide the clearest surfaced independent discussion in the batch; the paper spans three core AI categories.

sections.title: StepBack: Step-Level Error-Localized Resampling for Efficient Test-Time Reasoning
sections.abstract: StepBack locates likely first-error steps in a small set of reasoning drafts and resamples each error step and suffix, matching self-consistency accuracy on average across seven math and multi-hop QA benchmarks while using up to 41.26% fewer tokens.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors propose error-localized suffix resampling as a complement to sampling fewer full trajectories, reporting average accuracy comparable to self-consistency with lower token use.
sections.unique_caveat: The authors focus on NLL- and PRM-based localization signals and state that transfer to domains such as code generation and long-context summarization remains untested.
sections.evidence_for_ranking: The arXiv record lists NeurIPS 2026; same-day technical coverage, a three-category cross-list, and a seven-benchmark evaluation provide additional signals.

sections.title: Benchmarks as Software: Terminal-Bench and the Case for Continuous Benchmarks
sections.abstract: The paper proposes ongoing validation and human-gated repair for agent benchmarks; its audit of Terminal-Bench 2.0 finds defects in about 30% of tasks, with repairs raising accuracy by over 10 points and shifting some leaderboard positions by up to three places.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors define benchmark maintenance debt and show a workflow combining reports, traces, automated checks, and human-reviewed fixes; they also report a 0.958 Spearman correlation between old and repaired overall rankings.
sections.unique_caveat: The authors' external-validity audit covered 34 sampled Harbor-Index tasks and still missed defects, motivating benchmark-specific checks and domain expertise.
sections.evidence_for_ranking: The paper reports quantified changes to benchmark accuracy and rankings, plus evidence that time budgets alter agent comparisons; included for demonstrated evaluation relevance.

sections.title: SwarmEvolve: Latent Agent Swarms for Evolutionary Discovery and Optimization
sections.abstract: SwarmEvolve uses swarms of low-cost agents that exchange KV caches and evolve candidate programs in latent space; on 21 mathematical and scientific-computing problems, the authors report reaching comparable best scores in a median of 3–8 minutes versus 60 minutes for other tested frameworks.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors replace repeated natural-language generation with latent-space swarm communication, hidden-state novelty filtering, and KV-cache crossover for program search.
sections.unique_caveat: The reported speed and score comparisons are bounded to the paper's 21 selected problems and tested framework/model setup; broader scientific tasks remain to be evaluated.
sections.evidence_for_ranking: The AI and neural/evolutionary-computing cross-list and a concrete 21-problem evaluation make this a strong methods signal in the batch.

sections.title: La-JEPA: Compact Robot Policies with Latent World Modeling
sections.abstract: La-JEPA trains a compact action policy in pretrained V-JEPA feature space and reports strong simulation results plus average success comparable to pi0.5 on four real-robot tasks, while generating actions rather than video at inference.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors argue that control-specific policy architecture can outperform larger generation-derived policies in their evaluated settings, and report that JEPA features help especially out of distribution.
sections.unique_caveat: The real-robot comparison covers four tasks, and the authors note that the official LIBERO-Plus evaluator corrupts instructions for most variants; they correct and re-evaluate several baselines.
sections.evidence_for_ranking: Three-category breadth, simulation and real-robot experiments, and coverage from Physical AI News support its inclusion as a notable robotics paper.

sections.title: OopsieRecover: Learning Transferable VLA Corrections from Semantic Interventions
sections.abstract: OopsieRecover infers the intent behind a small set of corrective demonstrations and converts it into spatial representations and conditional costs, with the authors reporting transfer of VLA recovery behavior across six tasks and scene variations.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors use abductive inference to turn a handful of corrective examples into semantic constraints that can guide a frozen VLA policy in situations not directly demonstrated.
sections.unique_caveat: The abstract reports experiments on six tasks; robustness outside those tasks and variation types is not established by this submission.
sections.evidence_for_ranking: A concrete embodied-agent contribution evaluated across task, object-pose, and scene variations, adding an applied robotics result to a batch with several language-model papers.

sections.title: Measured Coupling for Parallel Decoding in Diffusion Language Models
sections.abstract: The paper measures how committing one token changes confidence at other positions and uses those couplings to guide diffusion-LM parallel decoding, reporting fewer decoding steps and faster runs on three models and four benchmarks at an average accuracy cost of 1.1 points.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors replace a similarity-based proxy with measured token-confidence coupling using probes within the main forward pass, without additional training or a separate model.
sections.unique_caveat: The reported speedup comes with an average 1.1-point accuracy reduction and is evaluated on three models and four benchmarks.
sections.evidence_for_ranking: A broad cross-list across language, AI, systems, and ML plus a controlled multi-model/multi-benchmark evaluation make this a strong inference-systems result.

sections.title: Agent-R²: Scaling Agents for Realistic Productivity Work via Real-Source Data Synthesis
sections.abstract: Agent-R² synthesizes productivity tasks from occupational seeds, workflow evidence, and authentic files, then trains a 4B model on 4,000 instances; the authors report higher results than Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking-2507 on GDPval and OfficeQA.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors combine real-source task synthesis, supervised fine-tuning, and rubric-based reinforcement learning to target realistic file-based work and reduce superficially plausible but ungrounded deliverables.
sections.unique_caveat: The reported benchmark advantage is limited to GDPval and OfficeQA; broader occupations, file types, and independent replication remain open.
sections.evidence_for_ranking: The deliverable-grounded task design and comparisons on two productivity benchmarks make this a notable practical-agent paper, linking training data to real-work outputs.

sections.title: Multimodal-SEA: Benchmarking AI Agent Security under Multimodal Social Engineering Attacks
sections.abstract: Multimodal-SEA supplies 608 simulated, expert-designed tasks across 14 domains and 152 attack scenarios; evaluations of seven models find attack success rates of 7.1–34.5%, with multimodal content increasing attack success in the reported setup.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors introduce an interactive multimodal red-team benchmark and harness for testing whether personal agents verify suspicious requests before acting.
sections.unique_caveat: The evaluation uses simulated applications and seven models; the attack rates do not establish real-world incident rates, and the authors also report excessive refusal for some models.
sections.evidence_for_ranking: The batch's applied agent-security benchmark, with concrete tool-execution outcomes and bilingual social-engineering scenarios.
